claims.text: The Rouen prosecutor's office said its main hypothesis is that a piece of rail on one track may have caused the derailment; it opened an inquiry and assigned it to Rouen judicial police.

event_overview.title: About 9/11 Victim Compensation
event_overview.subject: 9/11 Victim Compensation
event_overview.summary: The September 11th Victim Compensation Fund (VCF) is a federally funded, no-fault compensation program for people who suffered eligible physical harm or died as a result of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks or related debris-removal work. It is distinct from the World Trade Center Health Program: the VCF provides financial compensation, while the health program provides monitoring and treatment for certified conditions.

facts.label: Origins and duration
facts.value: Congress created the original fund in 2001; it operated from 2001 to 2004. The James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act reactivated it in 2011, and the 2019 permanent-authorization law set an October 1, 2090 claim-filing deadline and provides funding necessary for approved claims.

facts.label: Purpose and legal scope
facts.value: The VCF compensates eligible individuals, or personal representatives of those who died, for physical injury, illness, or death connected to the September 11 attacks or immediate post-attack debris removal; it is designed as an alternative to tort litigation.

facts.label: Covered locations and periods
facts.value: For presence eligibility, the program recognizes the World Trade Center and surrounding New York City Exposure Zone from September 11, 2001 through May 30, 2002; the Pentagon site through November 19, 2001; and the Shanksville, Pennsylvania site through October 3, 2001.

facts.label: Administration
facts.value: The fund is administered by the U.S. Department of Justice, with a Special Master appointed by the Attorney General and operational support from DOJ's Civil Division.

facts.label: Relationship to health benefits
facts.value: VCF eligibility generally requires an eligible physical health condition and proof of presence; World Trade Center Health Program certification is accepted as proof of an eligible condition subject to other requirements. Enrollment in the health program does not automatically register someone with the VCF.

explore_lenses.label: Why does compensation remain part of 9/11 remembrance?
explore_lenses.title: The toll includes illnesses diagnosed years later
explore_lenses.summary: Commemorations increasingly recognize people whose deaths or illnesses are linked to post-attack exposure, not only those killed on September 11, 2001. Federal health care and compensation systems remain active because eligible conditions can emerge long after exposure.

claims.text: The World Trade Center Health Program covers monitoring and medically necessary treatment for certified 9/11-related conditions, including specified cancers, respiratory and digestive conditions, mental-health conditions, and some responder musculoskeletal disorders.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: “Iran War” is a shorthand for the 2026 armed conflict centered on direct U.S.-Iran hostilities, Iranian attacks and alleged attacks involving states around the Persian Gulf, and disruptions to maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. The United States calls its campaign Operation Epic Fury and says it began to protect U.S. forces, regional partners and navigation; Iran has described the U.S. and Israeli actions as unlawful aggression.

facts.label: Start of direct U.S. operation
facts.value: U.S. Central Command says Operation Epic Fury against Iran began on February 28, 2026, at the President’s direction. In a March 10 letter to the UN Security Council, the United States said it had commenced combat operations on February 28 in cooperation with Israel.

facts.label: Parties and regional reach
facts.value: The conflict directly involves the United States and Iran, with the United States describing Israel as an ally in its initial operations. UN Security Council resolution 2817 (2026) addressed attacks attributed to Iran against Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan.

facts.label: Strategic waterway
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz lies between Iran and Oman and connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea. It is a major oil and liquefied-natural-gas transit chokepoint, so threats to shipping there can have wider energy-market effects.

facts.label: Competing legal positions
facts.value: The United States notified the Security Council that it was acting in self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter. Iran has told the Council that the U.S. and Israeli campaign constituted aggression and that subsequent Iranian measures were self-defense; these are opposing state positions, not a judicial determination.

facts.label: U.S. constitutional and statutory contex
facts.value: Under the War Powers Resolution, U.S. policy is that the collective judgment of Congress and the President should apply to the introduction and continued use of U.S. armed forces in hostilities; the statute identifies a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by attack as bases for introducing forces into hostilities.

facts.label: International legal framework
facts.value: UN Security Council Resolution 1695, adopted on July 15, 2006, demanded that the DPRK suspend activities related to its ballistic-missile program and called on UN member states to prevent transfers supporting DPRK missile or weapons-of-mass-destruction programs.

facts.label: UN sanctions regime
facts.value: Security Council Resolution 1718, adopted on October 14, 2006, established sanctions measures that include prohibitions intended to prevent the DPRK from conducting ballistic-missile launches, as well as an arms embargo, asset freezes and travel restrictions for designated persons.

facts.label: Oversight body
facts.value: The UN Security Council’s 1718 Committee oversees sanctions relating to the DPRK; its mandate includes measures addressing materials, technology and support that could contribute to the DPRK’s nuclear or ballistic-missile programs.

facts.label: Geographic context
facts.value: The missile-launch and exercise reporting is centered on the Korean Peninsula and its surrounding region, where the ROK–U.S. alliance conducts combined readiness exercises and the DPRK’s missile activity is monitored as a regional-security issue.

event_overview.subject: BRICS Summit
event_overview.summary: The BRICS Summit is the leaders’ meeting of BRICS, a political and diplomatic coordination forum of major emerging and developing economies that works across global governance, economic and financial cooperation, and people-to-people exchanges. facts.label: Dates and venue
facts.value: The 18th BRICS Summit is scheduled for 12–13 September 2026 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, India.

facts.label: Host and chairship
facts.value: India holds the 2026 BRICS chairship and is hosting the summit; its stated chairship theme is “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.”

facts.label: Membership
facts.value: BRICS has 11 full members: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Institutional form
facts.value: BRICS is an informal coordination mechanism rather than a treaty-based organization: it has no constitutive treaty, permanent secretariat or independent budget, and its presidency rotates among members.

facts.label: Participation and decisions
facts.value: Full members participate in all BRICS meetings and make decisions by consensus; partner countries may be invited to leaders’ and foreign-ministers’ meetings and other sessions subject to member consultation and consensus.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: “Iran War” is a shorthand for the 2026 armed conflict centered on direct U.S.-Iran hostilities, Iranian attacks and alleged attacks involving states around the Persian Gulf, and disruptions to maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. The United States calls its campaign Operation Epic Fury and says it began to protect U.S. forces, regional partners and navigation; Iran has described the U.S. and Israeli actions as unlawful aggression.

facts.label: Start of direct U.S. operation
facts.value: U.S. Central Command says Operation Epic Fury against Iran began on February 28, 2026, at the President’s direction. In a March 10 letter to the UN Security Council, the United States said it had commenced combat operations on February 28 in cooperation with Israel.

facts.label: Parties and regional reach
facts.value: The conflict directly involves the United States and Iran, with the United States describing Israel as an ally in its initial operations. UN Security Council resolution 2817 (2026) addressed attacks attributed to Iran against Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan.

facts.label: Strategic waterway
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz lies between Iran and Oman and connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea. It is a major oil and liquefied-natural-gas transit chokepoint, so threats to shipping there can have wider energy-market effects.

facts.label: Competing legal positions
facts.value: The United States notified the Security Council that it was acting in self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter. Iran has told the Council that the U.S. and Israeli campaign constituted aggression and that subsequent Iranian measures were self-defense; these are opposing state positions, not a judicial determination.

facts.label: U.S. constitutional and statutory contex
facts.value: Under the War Powers Resolution, U.S. policy is that the collective judgment of Congress and the President should apply to the introduction and continued use of U.S. armed forces in hostilities; the statute identifies a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by attack as bases for introducing forces into hostilities.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a limited set of developments from July 22-27, 2026—military threats, congressional war-powers action, shipping and oil-market pressure, Houthi claims, and ceasefire diplomacy—not the conflict’s full origins, all operations, or its eventual outcome.

event_overview.subject: Romance Scams
event_overview.summary: This event concerns the extradition from South Africa to the United States of six Nigerian nationals accused of participating in a Cape Town-based online-fraud operation. U.S. prosecutors allege that the operation used false online identities and purported romantic relationships, among other schemes, to obtain and launder victims’ money; the allegations have not been adjudicated and the defendants are presumed innocent.

facts.label: Alleged scheme period
facts.value: The U.S. charges describe an alleged conspiracy operating from at least 2011 through 2021.

facts.label: Locations and court
facts.value: The alleged operation was based in Cape Town, South Africa, targeted victims in the United States, and was charged in two federal cases before the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey in Trenton.

facts.label: Participants
facts.value: The underlying 2021 U.S. announcement charged eight Nigerian nationals, including alleged leaders of the Cape Town Zone of the Neo Black Movement of Africa, also known as Black Axe; South African authorities said six nationals were being transferred in September 2026.

facts.label: Alleged conduct and losses
facts.value: Authorities allege the defendants used romance scams and advance-fee schemes, as well as laundering connected to business-email-compromise fraud; South African authorities said more than 100 U.S. women were allegedly defrauded of over R100 million, reported as more than $6 million.

facts.label: Legal and extradition process
facts.value: The principal U.S. allegations include wire-fraud conspiracy and money-laundering conspiracy; the defendants were arrested in South Africa in 2021, and the Hawks and INTERPOL South Africa facilitated their September 2026 handover to U.S. authorities.

facts.label: Membership
facts.value: BRICS has 11 full members: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Institutional form
facts.value: BRICS is an informal coordination mechanism rather than a treaty-based organization: it has no constitutive treaty, permanent secretariat or independent budget, and its presidency rotates among members.

facts.label: Participation and decisions
facts.value: Full members participate in all BRICS meetings and make decisions by consensus; partner countries may be invited to leaders’ and foreign-ministers’ meetings and other sessions subject to member consultation and consensus.

event_overview.title: About 9/11 Victim Compensation
event_overview.subject: 9/11 Victim Compensation
event_overview.summary: The September 11th Victim Compensation Fund (VCF) is a federally funded, no-fault compensation program for people who suffered eligible physical harm or died as a result of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks or related debris-removal work. It is distinct from the World Trade Center Health Program: the VCF provides financial compensation, while the health program provides monitoring and treatment for certified conditions.

facts.label: Origins and duration
facts.value: Congress created the original fund in 2001; it operated from 2001 to 2004. The James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act reactivated it in 2011, and the 2019 permanent-authorization law set an October 1, 2090 claim-filing deadline and provides funding necessary for approved claims.

facts.label: Purpose and legal scope
facts.value: The VCF compensates eligible individuals, or personal representatives of those who died, for physical injury, illness, or death connected to the September 11 attacks or immediate post-attack debris removal; it is designed as an alternative to tort litigation.

facts.label: Covered locations and periods
facts.value: For presence eligibility, the program recognizes the World Trade Center and surrounding New York City Exposure Zone from September 11, 2001 through May 30, 2002; the Pentagon site through November 19, 2001; and the Shanksville, Pennsylvania site through October 3, 2001.

facts.label: Administration
facts.value: The fund is administered by the U.S. Department of Justice, with a Special Master appointed by the Attorney General and operational support from DOJ's Civil Division.

facts.label: Relationship to health benefits
facts.value: VCF eligibility generally requires an eligible physical health condition and proof of presence; World Trade Center Health Program certification is accepted as proof of an eligible condition subject to other requirements. Enrollment in the health program does not automatically register someone with the VCF.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers anniversary-related advocacy and commemoration connected to 9/11 victims; it does not attempt to track every VCF claim, award, health-program development, or related lawsuit.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: “Iran War” is a shorthand for the 2026 armed conflict centered on direct U.S.-Iran hostilities, Iranian attacks and alleged attacks involving states around the Persian Gulf, and disruptions to maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. The United States calls its campaign Operation Epic Fury and says it began to protect U.S. forces, regional partners and navigation; Iran has described the U.S. and Israeli actions as unlawful aggression.

facts.label: Start of direct U.S. operation
facts.value: U.S. Central Command says Operation Epic Fury against Iran began on February 28, 2026, at the President’s direction. In a March 10 letter to the UN Security Council, the United States said it had commenced combat operations on February 28 in cooperation with Israel.

facts.label: Parties and regional reach
facts.value: The conflict directly involves the United States and Iran, with the United States describing Israel as an ally in its initial operations. UN Security Council resolution 2817 (2026) addressed attacks attributed to Iran against Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan.

facts.label: Strategic waterway
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz lies between Iran and Oman and connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea. It is a major oil and liquefied-natural-gas transit chokepoint, so threats to shipping there can have wider energy-market effects.

facts.label: Competing legal positions
facts.value: The United States notified the Security Council that it was acting in self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter. Iran has told the Council that the U.S. and Israeli campaign constituted aggression and that subsequent Iranian measures were self-defense; these are opposing state positions, not a judicial determination.

facts.label: U.S. constitutional and statutory contex
facts.value: Under the War Powers Resolution, U.S. policy is that the collective judgment of Congress and the President should apply to the introduction and continued use of U.S. armed forces in hostilities; the statute identifies a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by attack as bases for introducing forces into hostilities.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a limited set of developments from July 22-27, 2026—military threats, congressional war-powers action, shipping and oil-market pressure, Houthi claims, and ceasefire diplomacy—not the conflict’s full origins, all operations, or its eventual outcome.
